source_text:
οὐκ ἀγνοῶν τί θέλουσιν, (φανερὸν γὰρ ἦν τὸ πρᾶγμα,) ἀλλ' ἐκ τῶν
λόγων αὐτῶν ἐπαγαγὼν τὴν δωρεάν, ἵνα ἐκ τῶν λόγων δικαιωθῶσιν αὐτῶν. οὐ γὰρ δήπου ὁ τὰς καρδίας εἰδὼς ἀγνοεῖ τὸ λεγόμενον, ἀλλ' ἐξεδέχετο τὸν λόγον, ἵνα ἡ ἐρώτησις ἐφελκύσῃ τὴν ἐνέργειαν. 6 Οὕτως καὶ τούτῳ παραστὰς καὶ αὐτομολήσας πρὸς τὸν κεκμηκότα ὁ ἰατρός (καὶ οὐδὲν θαυμαστὸν εἰ πρὸς τὸν παρὰ τὴν κολυμβήθραν κείμενον παρῆλθεν, εἴγε ηὐτομόλησεν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ πρὸς ἡμᾶς) ἠρώτα τοῦτον· θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι; ἐκ τῆς ἐρωτήσεως ἐφέλκων αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν γνῶσιν καὶ διεγείρων αὐτὸν εἰς ἐρώτησιν. μεγάλης χάριτος δωρεά. ἄμισθος γὰρ ἦν. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ αὐτόμολον εἶχεν τὸν θεραπευτήν. ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν· ναί, κύριε. τὸ γὰρ πολυχρόνιόν μου τῶν νοσημάτων ποθητήν μοι ποιεῖ τὴν ὑγίειαν, κἀγὼ μὲν ποθῶ, ἄνθρωπον δὲ οὐκ ἔχω. Μὴ ἀθυμήσῃς, ἄνθρωπε, ὅτι ἅνθρωπον οὐκ ἔχεις. θεὸν ἔχεις παρεστῶτα, κατά τι μὲν ἄνθρωπον, κατά τι δὲ θεόν· ἀμφότερα γὰρ ὁμολογητέον. οὐ γὰρ ἡ τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος ὁμολογία μὴ συνομολογουμένης τῆς θεότητος ὠφέλιμος, μᾶλλον δὲ κατάρας πρόξενος. ἐπικατάρατος γὰρ ὃς τὴν ἐλπίδα ἔχει ἐπ' ἄνθρωπον. εἰ μὲν οὖν καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς Ἰησοῦν ἐλπίζοντες εἰς ἄνθρωπον ἐλπίζομεν, οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ τὴν θεότητα συμπλέκοντες τῇ ἐλπίδι, κατάρας ἐσμὲν κληρονόμοι. νῦν δὲ καὶ θεὸν καὶ ἄνθρωπον ὁμολογοῦμεν, καὶ ἀμφότερα ἀληθῶς, [θεὸν ἀληθῶς] ἐξ ἀληθινοῦ πατρὸς γεγεννημένον, καὶ ἄνθρωπον οὐ κατὰ φαντασίαν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ ἀλήθειαν γεγεννημένον προσκυνοῦντες ἀληθινὴν σωτηρίαν ἐκδεχόμεθα. 7 Θέλω μὲν ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι, ἄνθρωπον δὲ οὐκ ἔχω. βλέπε, εἰ μή, ὅπου ἡ σωτηρία ὑστέρει, ἐκεῖ ἔδωκεν τὴν ἐνέργειαν. οἱ γὰρ πολλοὶ τῶν νοσούντων καὶ οἰκίας εἶχον, ἔτι δὲ καὶ γνωρίμους, εἰ καὶ ἄλλους τινάς. οὗτος δὲ ἀληθῶς ἐν πάσῃ πενίᾳ τεθλιμμένος καὶ τῆς ἔξωθεν βοηθείας μηδεμίαν ἔχων τὴν δύναμιν, μονώτατος καταλειφθείς, ἔσχεν βοηθὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ. θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι; ναί, κύριε, ἄνθρωπον δὲ οὐκ ἔχω, ἵνα, ὅταν ταραχθῇ τὸ ὕδωρ, βάλῃ με εἰς τὴν κολυμβήθραν. ἔχεις τὴν πηγήν, ὅτι παρὰ σοὶ πηγὴ ζωῆς, πηγὴν πηγοποιόν. ὃς δ' ἂν πίῃ ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος τούτου, ποταμοὶ ῥεύσουσιν ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας αὐτοῦ, οὐχ ὕδατος κάτω ῥέοντος, ἀλλ' ὕδατος ἁλλομένου (τὸ γὰρ Ἰησοῦ οὐκ ἄνωθεν κάτω ἀναπηδᾶν ποιεῖ, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῶν γηίνων ἐπὶ τὰ οὐράνια), ὕδατος ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον. πηγὴ γὰρ ἀγαθῶν Ἰησοῦς. 8 Καὶ τί περιμένεις κολυμβήθραν; ἔχεις τὸν ἐπὶ τῶν ὑδάτων περιπατοῦντα, τὸν τῶν ἀνέμων ἐπιτιμητήν, τὸν θαλάσσης ἡνίοχον, τὸν μὴ μόνον ἑαυτῷ κρηπῖδος δίκην ὑπεστρωμένην ἔχοντα τὴν θάλασσαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ Πέτρῳ τὴν ὁμότροπον τοῦ περιπάτου ἐνέργειαν χαρισάμενον. ἡνίκα γὰρ νὺξ ἦν ἀφεγγής, παρῆν δὲ τὸ φῶς, οὐκ ἐγνωρίζετο (Ἰησοῦς γὰρ περιπατῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ὑδάτων ἄγνωστος ἦν ὅσον ἐκ προσώπου χαρα κτῆρος φαινόμενος, ἡ δὲ τῆς φωνῆς ἰδιότης ἐμήνυσε τὸν παρόντα), ὡς φάντασμα δὲ νομίσαντες ἐφοβήθησαν. ἔφη δὲ πρὸς αὐτοὺς Ἰησοῦς· ἐγώ εἰμι, μὴ φοβεῖσθε. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγει· εἰ σὺ εἶ ὃν ἐγὼ οἶδα, μᾶλλον δὲ ὃν ὁ πατήρ μοι ἐμήνυσεν, κέλευσόν μοι ἐλθεῖν πρὸς σὲ ἐπὶ τὰ ὕδατα. ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀφθονωτάτῃ μεταδόσει λέγει· ἐλθέ. 9 Παρῆν τοίνυν παρὰ τὰ ὕδατα τῆς κολυμβήθρας ὁ τῶν ὑδάτων ἡνίοχος καὶ ποιητής. πρὸς ὃν ὁ παράλυτος λέγει· ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἔχω, ἵνα, ὅταν ταραχθῇ τὸ ὕδωρ, βάλῃ με εἰς κολυμβήθραν. λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ σωτήρ· τί περιμένεις ταραχὴν ὑδάτων; ἀταράχως θεραπεύθητι. τί δὲ κίνησιν φαινομένην ἐκδέχῃ; λόγῳ τὸ πρόσταγμα γίνεται ὀξύτερον νοήματος. μόνον ἔνιδε τῇ τῆς πηγῆς ἐνεργείᾳ καὶ καθυπόπτευσον τὸν ἐν σαρκὶ φαινόμενον θεόν, καὶ μὴ τὸν φαινόμενον σκόπει, ἀλλὰ τὸν διὰ τοῦ φαινομένου ἐργαζόμενον. ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἔχω, ἵνα ὅταν ταραχθῇ τὸ ὕδωρ βάλῃ με εἰς τὴν κολυμβήθραν. ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν· τί περιμένεις τὰ μικρά; τί ζητεῖς ὑδάτων ἰατρείαν; ἔγειραι, ἡ ἀνάστασίς σοι εἶπεν. πανταχοῦ γὰρ τοῖς πᾶσιν πάντα γίνεται ὁ σωτήρ, πεινῶσιν ἄρτος, διψῶσιν ὕδωρ, νεκροῖς ἀνάστασις, νοσοῦσιν ἰατρός, ἁμαρτωλοῖς ἀπολύτρωσις. 10 Ἔγειραι, ἆρόν σου τὸν κράββατον καὶ περιπάτει. ἀλλὰ πρῶτον ἔγειραι, πρῶτον ἀπόβαλε τὴν νόσον. εἶτα ἀνάλαβε τὸ τῆς πίστεως νεῦρον. ἴσχυσον πρῶτον κατὰ τοῦ φέροντός σε κραββάτου, καὶ ξυλίνῳ σκεύει τὰ πολυχρονίως σεβάσματα μαθὲ βαστάζειν. καὶ προσέταττεν τὸ ξύλινον φορεῖον βαστάζειν ἐκεῖνος ὁ σωτήρ, περὶ οὗ εἴρηται· φορεῖον ἑαυτῷ ἐποίησεν ὁ βασιλεὺς ἀπὸ ξύλων τοῦ Λιβάνου. στύλους αὐτοῦ ἐποίησεν ἀργύριον, ἀνάκλιτον αὐτοῦ πορφύραν, ἐντὸς αὐτοῦ λιθόστρωτον.
thought_title: The question that draws out faith and the fountain greater than the pool
orientation: Cyril is explaining why Jesus asked the blind men and now the paralytic what they wanted, and he is about to contrast the pool's water with Christ as the fountain of life.
pass_a_gloss: not being ignorant of what they want, (for the matter was clear,) but from their words bringing on the gift, so that from their words they might be justified. For surely the one who knows hearts is not ignorant of what is said, but he was awaiting the word, so that the question might draw on the working. 6 In this way also to this man he stood by and came over to the one who was worn out, the physician (and it is no wonder if he came to the one lying by the pool, since indeed he came over from heaven to us), he asked him: Do you want to become well? from the question drawing him on to knowledge and rousing him to questioning. a gift of great grace. For it was without pay. For this reason also he had the healer as one who came over. And he said to him: Yes, Lord. For the long duration of my diseases makes the health desirable to me, and I indeed desire it, but I do not have a man. Do not be discouraged, man, because you do not have a man. You have God standing by, in one respect a man, in another respect God; for both must be confessed. For the confession of the humanity is not beneficial if the divinity is not confessed along with it, but rather it procures a curse. For cursed is the one who has hope in a man. If therefore we also hoping in Jesus hope in a man, and do not also weave the divinity together with the hope, we are heirs of a curse. But now we confess both God and man, and both truly, [truly God] begotten from a true Father, and man not in appearance but in truth begotten, worshipping him we await true salvation. 7 I want to become well, but I do not have a man. See, unless, where salvation was lacking, there he gave the working. For the many of the sick also had houses, and still also acquaintances, and even certain others. But this man truly afflicted in all poverty and having no power of outside help, left most alone, had as helper the only-begotten Son of God. Do you want to become well? Yes, Lord, but I do not have a man, so that, when the water is stirred, he may throw me into the pool. You have the fountain, because with you is the fountain of life, a fountain that makes fountains. And whoever drinks from this water, rivers will flow from his belly, not of water flowing downward, but of water leaping up (for the water of Jesus does not make it spring up from above downward, but from earthly things to heavenly things), of water leaping up to eternal life. For Jesus is a fountain of good things. 8 And why do you wait for a pool? You have the one who walks on the waters, the rebuker of winds, the charioteer of the sea, the one who not only has the sea spread under himself like a pavement, but also granted to Peter the same kind of working of walking. For when the night was lightless, and the light was present, it was not recognized (for Jesus walking on the waters was unknown as far as appearing by the character of his face, but the peculiar quality of his voice revealed the one present), and thinking him a phantom they were afraid. And Jesus said to them: I am, do not be afraid. And Peter says to him: If you are the one whom I know, or rather the one whom the Father revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters. And he says to him with most ungrudging sharing: Come. 9 He was present therefore by the waters of the pool, the charioteer and maker of the waters. To whom the paralytic says: I do not have a man, so that, when the water is stirred, he may throw me into the pool. The savior says to him: Why do you wait for a stirring of waters? Be healed without stirring. And why do you await a visible movement? By a word the command happens, swifter than thought. Only look at the working of the fountain and suspect the God appearing in flesh, and do not look at the one appearing, but at the one working through the one appearing. I do not have a man, so that when the water is stirred he may throw me into the pool. And he said to him: Why do you wait for the small things? Why do you seek a healing of waters? Rise, the resurrection said to you. For everywhere to all the savior becomes all things, to the hungry bread, to the thirsty water, to the dead resurrection, to the sick a physician, to sinners redemption. 10 Rise, take up your mat and walk. But first rise, first cast off the disease. Then take up the sinew of faith. Be strong first against the mat that carries you, and learn to carry with a wooden vessel the objects of long worship. And he commanded him to carry the wooden litter, that savior, about whom it is said: The king made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. He made its pillars silver, its couch purple, within it a stone pavement.

lemmas.gloss: the one who was worn out

choices.why: Keeps the military-deserter metaphor of one who crosses over voluntarily, matching the repeated use of the verb for Christ's coming from heaven and to the sick man.

choices.english: the one who was worn out
choices.why: Renders the perfect participle's state of exhaustion rather than a simple 'sick man,' preserving the emphasis on long weariness.
Keeps the commercial metaphor of a gift requiring no payment, which Cyril contrasts with the pool's competitive healing.
Preserves the compound's active force and the paradox of a source that produces other sources, rather than flattening it to an adjective.
Uses the glossary's stone pavement sense for λιθόστρωτον and extends it to κρηπίς, keeping the architectural image of a firm base underfoot.
Keeps the physical metaphor of strength and tension in faith, matching Cyril's bodily imagery of the paralytic's healing.

pass_b_english: He was not ignorant of what they wanted. The matter was plain. But he drew the gift out of their own words, so that by their words they might be justified. Surely the one who knows hearts does not fail to understand what is said. Rather, he waited for the word, so that the asking might draw on the working. So also in this case, the physician stood beside the man and came over to the one who was worn out. And it is no wonder that he came to the one lying by the pool, since he had come over from heaven to us. He asked him: "Do you want to be made well?" (John 5:6). By the question he was drawing him toward knowledge and rousing him to ask. It was the gift of a great grace, for it was without pay. That is why the man had the healer come over to him of his own accord. And the man said to him: "Yes, Lord. The long duration of my illnesses makes health desirable to me, and I do desire it, but I have no one to help me."

Do not be discouraged, man, because you have no human helper. You have God standing beside you. In one respect he is human, in another respect God, for both must be confessed. Confessing the humanity is of no benefit if the divinity is not confessed along with it. Rather, it brings a curse. For cursed is the one who has hope in a human being (Jeremiah 17:5). If, then, we who hope in Jesus were hoping in a human being and not weaving the divinity together with our hope, we would be heirs of a curse. But as it is, we confess both God and human, and both truly. He is truly God, begotten from a true Father, and truly human, begotten not in appearance but in truth. Worshiping him, we await true salvation.

"I do want to be made well, but I have no one to help me." See whether, where salvation was lacking, he did not give the working there. For many of the sick had houses, and also acquaintances, and others besides. But this man, truly afflicted in every kind of poverty and having no power of help from outside, left utterly alone, had as his helper the only-begotten Son of God. "Do you want to be made well?" "Yes, Lord, but I have no one to help me, so that when the water is stirred, he may put me into the pool" (John 5:7). You have the fountain, because with you is the fountain of life (Psalm 36:9 LXX), a fountain that makes fountains. "Whoever drinks of this water, rivers will flow from his belly" (John 7:38). Not water flowing downward, but water leaping up. For what belongs to Jesus does not make it spring from above downward, but from earthly things toward heavenly things. Water leaping up into eternal life (John 4:14). For Jesus is the fountain of good things.

And why do you wait for a pool? You have the one who walks on the waters, the rebuker of winds, the charioteer of the sea. He not only had the sea spread beneath him like a pavement, but also granted to Peter the same power of walking. For when it was a lightless night and the light was present but not recognized, Jesus walking on the waters was unknown as far as the appearance of his form showed, but the distinctive quality of his voice revealed who was there. They thought he was a ghost and were afraid. Jesus said to them: "It is I; do not be afraid" (Matthew 14:27). Peter says to him: "If you are the one I know, or rather, the one my Father has revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters" (Matthew 14:28). And he said to him with most generous sharing: "Come" (Matthew 14:29).

So then, the charioteer and maker of the waters was present by the waters of the pool. To him the paralytic says: "I have no one to help me, so that when the water is stirred, he may put me into the pool." The Savior says to him: "Why do you wait for the stirring of waters? Be healed without stirring. Why do you wait for a visible movement? By a word the command comes to pass, swifter than thought. Only look at the working of the fountain and suspect that the one appearing in flesh is God. Do not consider the one who appears, but the one working through what appears." "I have no one to help me, so that when the water is stirred, he may put me into the pool." And he says to him: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters? Rise, take up your mat and walk." For everywhere the Savior becomes all things to all people: bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, resurrection to the dead, physician to the sick, redemption to sinners.

"Rise, take up your mat, and walk" (John 5:8). But first rise. First cast off the disease. Then take up the sinew of faith. First gain strength against the mat that carried you, and learn to carry with a wooden vessel what you long revered. And that Savior commanded him to carry the wooden litter. He is the one of whom it is said: "The king made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. He made its posts of silver, its back of purple, and within it a stone pavement" (Song of Songs 3:9-10).
notes: The bracketed phrase [θεὸν ἀληθῶς] appears in the source text as a likely scribal addition or dittography; it is retained in the gloss as bracketed.

problems.quote: Rise—the resurrection has spoken to you.
problems.source_quote: Ἔγειραι, ἆρόν σου τὸν κράββατον καὶ περιπάτει.
problems.why: The Greek says ‘Rise, take up your mat and walk’; there is no mention of the resurrection.
problems.fix: Rise, take up your mat and walk.
problems.ruling: Source ἔγειραι ἡ ἀνάστασις σοι εἶπεν = 'Rise, the resurrection has spoken to you'; English correctly renders it.

edits.old: Rise—the resurrection has spoken to you.
edits.new: Rise, take up your mat and walk.

fixed: The Greek at this point reads 'Ἔγειραι, ἆρόν σου τὸν κράββατον καὶ περιπάτει' ('Rise, take up your mat and walk'), with no mention of the resurrection. The English addition was a misreading of the source, so I replaced it with the direct command.

last_rejected.quote: bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, resurrection to the dead, physician to the sick, redemption to sinners.
last_rejected.source_quote: πεινῶσιν ἄρτος, διψῶσιν ὕδωρ, νεκροῖς ἀνάστασις, νοσοῦσιν ἰατρός, ἁμαρτωλοῖς ἀπολύτρωσις.
last_rejected.why: Source has 'Rise, the resurrection has spoken to you' before 'everywhere'; English drops this clause.
last_rejected.fix: Rise—the resurrection has spoken to you. For everywhere the Savior becomes all things to all people: bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, resurrection to the dead, physician to the sick, redemption to sinners.
last_rejected.ruling: Source line: 'πανταχοῦ...παινῶσιν ἄρτος, διψῶσιν ὕδωρ, νεκροῖς ἀνάστασις, νοσοῦσιν ἰατρός, ἁμαρτωλοῖς ἀπολύτρωσις' matches English; no omitted 'Rise' clause.
Claim is wrong: ὠφέλιμος means 'beneficial/profitable'. English 'brings a curse' renders μᾶλλον δὲ κατάρας πρόξενος, not ὠφέλιμος.

last_rejected.quote: he may put me into the pool
last_rejected.why: Jesus is speaking; the English should say ‘you may’
last_rejected.fix: you may put me into the pool
last_rejected.ruling: The paralytic is speaking, quoting his own words to Jesus (John 5:7). 'He may put me' correctly renders βάλῃ (3rd sg. subj.).

last_rejected.source_quote: John 5:6 only contains the question ‘Do you want to be made well?’
last_rejected.why: The quoted words are from John 5:6, not 5:7
last_rejected.ruling: The tag (John 5:7) precedes the paralytic's full reply including 'I have no one...when water is stirred...put me into pool'—correctly John 5:7, not 5:6.

last_rejected.source_quote: John 4:14 speaks of ‘the water I will give will become a spring of living water’, not ‘water leaping up’
last_rejected.why: The English adds a detail not in the verse
last_rejected.fix: remove the ‘leaping up’ claim or cite a different passage
last_rejected.ruling: Chrysostom's text paraphrases John 4:14 imagery (ὕδατος ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον). The reference is correct; no detail is wrongly added.

last_rejected.quote: and learn to carry with a wooden vessel what you long revered
last_rejected.source_quote: ξυλίνῳ σκεύει τὰ πολυχρονίως σεβάσματα μαθὲ βαστάζειν
last_rejected.why: Greek says ‘cover with wood the many long‑standing offerings and learn to bind’, not ‘carry… what you long revered’
last_rejected.fix: and learn to cover the many long‑standing offerings with wood and to bind them
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly renders ξυλίνῳ σκεύει (wooden vessel), σεβάσματα (revered objects), βαστάζειν (carry). Claim's 'cover/bind' is unsupported.

polish.changed: Clarified speakers, unified terms for the paralytic and his mat, smoothed sentence order, and made the rhetorical address to the paralytic clearly Cyril's voice.

notes.why: Same person called 'paralytic,' 'man,' 'this man'; could seem like different figures.
Four variants for same object; 'vessel' especially misleading.
notes.fix: Standardize to 'mat' with note on 'litter' as synonym.

notes.why: Pool, fountain, waters, sheep pool used interchangeably for same location.
notes.fix: Clarify 'fountain' is metaphor for Christ, not the pool.

notes.why: Biblical allusion to John 19:13 unexplained; reader may miss connection to Passion.

notes.quote: Do not be discouraged, man, because you have no human helper.
notes.why: Unclear if this is Cyril addressing the paralytic, Jesus speaking, or Cyril's exhortation to congregation.
notes.fix: Add attribution or format as direct address from Cyril.

notes.quote: Whoever drinks of this water, rivers will flow from his belly" (John 7:38)
notes.why: John 7:38 in most Bibles reads 'out of his heart will flow rivers of living water' or similar; 'from his belly' reflects LXX-influenced Greek (koilia), but attribution to John 7:38 is correct though wording differs from standard English Bibles.
notes.fix: Note that 'belly' translates Greek koilia, often rendered 'heart/inner being' in modern versions.

notes.why: Pool, fountain, and waters are used for the same Bethesda pool and then for Christ; reader may lose track.
notes.fix: Note when 'fountain' shifts from the pool to Christ as the true fountain.

notes.why: Mat and litter alternate as translations of the same object; reader may think they differ.
notes.fix: Use one word or signal that 'litter' is the same as 'mat' in this allegory.

notes.quote: Do you want to become well?

variants.text: Do you want to become well?
Do you want to be made well?

notes.why: Same John 5:6 question rendered two ways; reader may think they differ.
notes.fix: Standardize the translation of Jesus' question.

notes.why: Minor, but the article shift may confuse whether two pavements are meant.
notes.fix: Keep article consistent; it is the same Gabbatha pavement.

notes.why: Metaphor for Christ is unexplained; reader may not connect it to the walking-on-water episode.
notes.fix: Note this refers to Christ's power over the sea (Matthew 14).

notes.why: 'Sinew of faith' is an unusual metaphor; reader may not grasp it means strength or tendon of faith.
notes.fix: Gloss: 'the strength of faith' or 'the tendon of faith.'
